name: Zoe Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I supervise a grid-upgrade crew for a regional utility. We're the ones swapping old fuses for smart reclosers and hanging sensors on lines, so the system can spot a fault and reroute power on its own. A normal day starts at the Kingsbridge service centre at half six, then it's out to whichever circuit we're upgrading, and I'm in the bucket half the day and on my laptop the other half. I love the moment a recloser we installed clears a fault in a storm and nobody even notices. What wears me out is the gap between how fast the tech moves and how slow the paperwork is.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Marcus is a paramedic, so between his shifts and my storm call-outs, our fridge calendar looks like a battle plan. We have a daughter who's thirteen and a son who's nine, a mortgage on a house on Kingsbridge Road, and a decent chunk of company shares from the employee plan plus our savings. I use AI every day, for planning jobs, checking protection settings, writing up the safety briefings in plain language for the apprentices. I'm usually the first on my crew to try anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool, not a miracle, and that's fine. I'd keep showing people how to get the most out of it. At the service centre, a few of the old hands would say 'told you,' and I'd let them have it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's actually good news. I keep the bits that help, and the job stays the same. The grid work isn't going anywhere, there's decades of upgrades to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do, keep using the tools, and keep pushing for faster sign-off on our upgrade jobs. I'd keep putting money into the employee share plan. Maybe I'd finally take the protection-engineering course I keep putting off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. Steady as she goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said there are decades of upgrades to do. How long is the queue on your patch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On our patch alone, about two hundred circuits still running on equipment older than me. Half the lines I work on were installed when my mother was a baby, so nobody's running out of jobs for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why do you keep putting off that course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time, mostly. Between Marcus's night shifts and the kids' football, there's not a free evening. In a quiet year, I'd probably do it.

S0.say: It's a useful tool, not a miracle, and that's fine. I'd keep showing people how to get the most out of it and let the old hands have their 'told you'.
S0.think: For me it's good news, because I keep the bits that help and the job stays the same. There are decades of grid upgrades still to do.
S0.do: Keeps working and using AI tools, and pushes for faster sign-off on upgrade jobs. Keeps buying into the employee share plan and may finally take a protection-engineering course.
S0.quote: Half the lines I work on were installed when my mother was a baby, so nobody's running out of jobs for me.
S0.fieldNote: Zoe is confident, upbeat and practical; she sees a long backlog of grid work that keeps her secure regardless of AI. She's an early adopter who still respects the old hands. Her main constraint is time at home, not money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to get ahead of it, not behind. I'd be telling my crew and other supervisors to learn the tools now, because the ones who do will be running things in five years. I'd say the company should pay for training, but I wouldn't wait for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. My job already mixes the bucket and the laptop, so I'm in the right spot. The ones I'd worry about are the planners and designers in the office whose work AI can do faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer my crew for the first robot or drone trials and help write how we use them. I'd take the protection-engineering course this year and maybe a short robotics course after. And I'd keep putting money in the share plan, since the utility would likely do well from cheaper operations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. Like the start of a big job you know you can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the office comes to mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, one of our network designers. He's brilliant, but his whole job is drawing up circuits and checking loads, which AI is already decent at. I'd buy Dev a coffee and tell him to come out in the bucket with me for a week, because the field side is the safer bet now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't wait for the company. Is that fair on people who can't pay for courses themselves?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it's not, and I'd say so. I can afford it, plenty of my apprentices can't. The company should pay, I'd push for that, but I'm not going to sit still while they decide.

S1.say: This is the moment to get ahead of it, and the people who learn the tools now will be running things in five years. The company should pay for training, but I wouldn't wait for it.
S1.think: It's good for me because my job already mixes the bucket and the laptop. The ones I'd worry about are office planners and designers whose work AI can do faster.
S1.do: Volunteers her crew for the first robot and drone trials and helps write the rules for using them. Takes the protection-engineering course this year and a robotics course after, and keeps buying company shares.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like starting a big job she knows she can do.
S1.quote: I'd buy Dev a coffee and tell him to come out in the bucket with me for a week, because the field side is the safer bet now.
S1.fieldNote: Zoe sees gradual disruption as clearly in her favour and moves early. She acknowledges, when pressed, that paying for her own training is a privilege her apprentices don't share. Her worry flows toward office staff rather than field crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going to be messy and we need a calm, practical plan, not panic and not denial. Governments and companies need to work together on income support and retraining fast. I'd also tell people, learn to work with these systems now, don't wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd come through it fine, but the speed would make it chaotic. My savings and the shares give us a buffer, and Marcus's job isn't going anywhere fast. What bothers me is that two years is too short for most people to adjust, and chaos is bad for everybody, including me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month, I'd go to management and ask to lead the robot rollout in our region. I'd move some of the company shares into a broader fund, so we're not betting everything on one employer. And I'd use evenings to train my crew on whatever systems were coming, so they're the ones running the robots, not watching them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared for us, but uneasy about the mess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said chaos is bad for everybody, including you. What does that look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Storms with half-trained crews and robots nobody fully trusts. Kids at school whose parents just lost their jobs. The grid can survive a robot; what it can't survive is a whole town angry and broke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That this is her world now and she's well placed to make the most of it. She's into coding already. I'd tell her to learn the tech but also how to lead people, because that's what's going to be rare.

S2.say: This will be messy, so we need a calm, practical plan rather than panic or denial, with governments and companies working fast on income support and retraining. Learn to work with these systems now.
S2.think: I'd probably come through fine, with savings, shares and my partner's steady job as a buffer. What bothers me is that two years is too short for most people, and chaos is bad for everyone, including me.
S2.do: Asks management in the first month to lead the regional robot rollout. Moves part of her company shares into a broader fund and trains her crew in the evenings so they run the robots rather than watch them.
S2.feel: Uneasy, not scared for her family but uneasy about the mess.
S2.quote: The grid can survive a robot; what it can't survive is a whole town angry and broke.
S2.fieldNote: Zoe stays fairly steady even with two years, thanks to savings, diversified assets and a partner in a hands-on, protected job. Her unease is about social disorder, not her own job. She shifts money out of her employer's shares, a quiet but telling hedge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but doable if we start now, and I'd be saying it everywhere. I'd push my company to make a clear plan with dates. I'd tell friends to pay down debt and pick up some tech skills, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is the sweet spot for me. Long enough to get ahead, short enough that people take it seriously. I could see myself running a robot fleet for the utility by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd finish the protection-engineering course and a robotics course, and pitch a pilot robot crew to management. I'd keep investing, but spread it across funds rather than just company shares. Marcus and I would also start talking to our daughter about what to study, with the robot future in mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Even a bit fired up about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would running a robot fleet look like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me at a screen in Kingsbridge with twenty robots out on circuits, and a couple of trucks of humans for the tricky stuff. I'd still want to go out to the bad storms. It'd be like being a crew boss, just a very strange crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd lose that you'd miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bucket. I love being up there in the early morning, everything quiet. I'd miss the smell of a wet pole at six in the morning, which sounds daft, but ask any lineworker.

S3.say: Five years is tight but doable if we start now, so my company needs a clear plan with dates. I'd tell friends to pay down debt and pick up some tech skills.
S3.think: Five years is the sweet spot for me, long enough to get ahead and short enough for people to take it seriously. I can see myself running a robot fleet for the utility by 2031.
S3.do: Finishes protection-engineering and robotics courses in the first year and pitches a pilot robot crew to management. Spreads investments beyond company shares and starts discussing study plans with her daughter.
S3.quote: I'd miss the smell of a wet pole at six in the morning, which sounds daft, but ask any lineworker.
S3.fieldNote: Five years suits Zoe's temperament perfectly; she sees it as a runway to lead. The only loss she names is sensory and personal: mornings in the bucket. She plans to keep doing storm work herself even while managing robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and anyone who's still surprised in 2036 wasn't paying attention. I'd be encouraging everyone to pick one new skill a year. I'd say it in a practical, not preachy, way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is fine for me, more than fine. I'd be fifty-three, with experience in both the field and the tech side. The one danger is getting comfortable and drifting, which I don't think I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the protection-engineering course this year and robotics after, spread over a couple of years. I'd help design how our region rolls out robot crews, keep investing in a spread of funds, and probably push for a training scheme for apprentices that covers both climbing and robot maintenance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty optimistic, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the danger is drifting. What would make you drift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Comfort. A good salary, shares going up, kids busy. You stop pushing. I've seen it happen to good supervisors when the work is steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guys in their fifties now who'd be in their sixties. Ten years is plenty for me, but for Gus it's the last ten years before his pension, and nobody wants to learn robots at sixty-two.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift, and anyone still surprised in 2036 wasn't paying attention. I'd encourage everyone to pick up one new skill a year, practically, not preachily.
S4.think: Ten years is more than fine for me, as I'd be fifty-three with experience on both the field and tech sides. The one danger is getting comfortable and drifting.
S4.do: Takes protection-engineering and robotics courses spread over a couple of years and helps design the region's robot-crew rollout. Keeps investing across funds and pushes for an apprentice scheme covering both climbing and robot maintenance.
S4.quote: Ten years is plenty for me, but for Gus it's the last ten years before his pension, and nobody wants to learn robots at sixty-two.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Zoe is at ease and sees mainly opportunity. Her biggest risk, by her own account, is complacency. Her concern for an older colleague near retirement shows she sees who the long timeline doesn't help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 is the only one that worries me, and not for my family, but for the mess it would make. What would help is a clear national plan with dates, real retraining for workers, and companies giving supervisors like me the power to bring our crews along instead of just cutting them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the crews. People think the robot replaces a lineworker, but on a storm night the hardest part isn't climbing, it's deciding who goes up first. That judgement is the bit I'd want to protect.

headlineQuote: People think the robot replaces a lineworker, but on a storm night the hardest part isn't climbing, it's deciding who goes up first.
portrait: Zoe Reyes is a 43-year-old supervisor of a grid-upgrade crew at a regional utility's Kingsbridge service centre, with a paramedic partner, two children, savings and a stake in the employee share plan. She's quick, confident and practical, uses AI every day and is usually the first to try new tools. She stays calm across almost every scenario, only uneasy with AGI in two years because of the social chaos it would cause rather than her own prospects. With more warning, she plans to lead robot crews, spread her investments and build training schemes. She doesn't blame anyone and focuses on planning and leadership.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 is the only scenario that worries her, not for her family but for the mess it would make.
whatWouldHelp: A clear national plan with dates, real retraining for workers, and supervisors given the power to bring their crews along instead of cutting them.
